2.text: because of their mental struggle against the call, that they are sometimes

3.text: said to sweat blood on the forehead and the temples. Afterwards every

4.text: preparation of a shaman for a performance is considered a sort of repetition

5.text: of the initiative process: hence it is said that the Chukchee shamans during

6.text: that time are easily susceptible to hemorrhage and even to bloody sweat.

7.text: I myself witnessed two cases of bleeding from the nose among Chukchee

8.text: shamans before their performances. As regards the bloody sweat, I knew

9.text: of only one case, and even in that I was suspicious that the shaman in

10.text: question, having an attack of nose-bleed, had happily thought to smear his

11.text: temples with blood in order to increase our respect for his shamanistic powers.

12.text: At least, he kept repeating that he was not like the modern shamans, but

13.text: that he was the equal of the ancient “genuine” shamans, who sweated blood

14.text: from the strain of their inspiration. He was, however, a typical specimen of

15.text: a Chukchee shaman, — a very unsteady, excitable nature; and after all, I

16.text: am not quite sure that he tricked us with his bloody sweat.

17.text: The preparatory period is compared by the Chukchee to a long, severe

18.text: illness; and the acquirement of inspiration, to a recovery. There are cases

19.text: of young persons who, having suffered for years from lingering illness (usually

20.text: of a nervous character), at last feel a call to take to shamanistic practice,

21.text: and by this means overcome the disease. Of course it is difficult to draw

22.text: the line of demarcation, and all these cases finally come under one and the

23.text: same class. The preparatory period of inspiration is designated by the Chuk-

24.text: chee by a special term, meaning “he gathers shamanistic power” (the verb

25.text: tewitɪˊñɪrkɪn and its derivatives). With weaker shamans and with women, the

26.text: preparatory period is less painful, and the call to inspiration comes mainly

28.text: To people of more mature age the shamanistic call may come during

29.text: some great misfortune, dangerous and protracted illness, sudden loss of family

30.text: or property, etc. Then the person, having no other resource, turns to the

31.text: “spirits,” and claims their assistance. It is generally considered that in such

32.text: cases a favorable issue is possible only with the aid of the “spirits:” there-

33.text: fore a man who has withstood some extraordinary trial of his life is con-

34.text: sidered as having within himself the possibilities of a shaman, and he often

35.text: feels bound to enter into closer relations with the “spirits,” lest he incur their

36.text: displeasure at his negligence and lack of gratitude.

37.text: This is evidenced in the case of Aiñanwaˊt, mentioned above. He was

38.text: not careful enough to obey the instructions of the “spirits,” who came to him

39.text: with benevolent intentions, and even performed upon him with a supernatural

40.text: silver knife of their own an operation which freed him from all diseased

41.text: matter. Hence, though he recovered from his illness, he had no further

42.text: good-fortune in life. He was unable to increase his diminished herd, and

43.text: after a few years of useless struggle found himself forced to bequeathe it,
